doc.title: Michael Max Fleming interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 8, 2017

title: First instruments: piano, accordion, doo-wop, then tuba in school
summary: Fleming moves from piano and accordion to doo-wop, then teaches himself tuba at 13 and gets school upright bass lessons. His uncle had promised him gigs if he had a bass.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: Well where did your method come from? Now was there a point in your life where you said, “I think that I could be a professional musician.”

I mean, because some people really know by the time they’re in fourth or fifth grade what they want to do, and often times it’s musicians. But some people, it’s later in life that they sort of fall into it. So I’m basically wondering, when did you take the path? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

Okay. My first instrument was piano and I just realized that in my community, as six year olds we had a band. All right. Later I went to accordion. When I went to accordion I had fantasies and visions of playing in front of people. And I just had visions of myself doing that. After that, after I stopped playing the accordion I was a doo-wopper, from the age of nine I could give everybody their parts. “Bobby you do [scats]” and “Johnny you do this.” At nine I could do that because my mother taught me as a six-year-old at the piano she would rehearse an imaginary choir. “Sopranos, altos.” So at a very young age I was exposed to that. But that went on and on and on. And my uncle, my mother’s youngest brother, was a virtuoso of many instruments. And he told me, he said, “Michael if we get you a bass I’ll take you on the gig with me.” Like that. I wanted to make money and have fun. So I went to the — I was in the seventh grade, eighth grade, tried to take up the upright bass. “Well sorry, right now we have enough bass players but if you would like I’ll teach you, you can play the tuba.” So at age 13 I started playing the tuba. Basically self-taught because the high school teacher, he was busy writing music for the spring show. So he said, “Here, you take this” — I can’t do it now. He gave me the mouthpiece, gave me the horn, showed me the first page. “If you have any questions just come back to my office and ask me.” So guess how many times I had to go back to him.
You had an ear for low notes.

Well I knew the bass clef from the piano and I had the instruction in the book. I played. So I played all through high school. I represented my school in the All-City Band Orchestra. But in the meanwhile now, okay, so there’s a lot. That was one high school, by the way it was the same high school that Frank Foster went to, and there’s another guy Fred, a piano player. I can’t think of his name. They both went to that same high school. But anyway so in the tenth grade the teacher tells me — you wonder when did I decide, I just tell you, the teacher, who was a bass player, said, “I need somebody for the spring concert.” So he showed me how to hold the bow. He gave me two lessons and said the same thing, sent me in the room where the instruments are kept. “If you have any questions come ask me.” But before that there was another school I went to where this teacher must have sent a note — he said, you know when you transfer from one school they said good student, does this, you know. I mean on that level I would think that teachers — because that teacher, and when I went to that teacher he locked me in a room too and gave me some tuba solos. “Hall of the Mountain King,” “The Marines Hymn” [scats]. At the end of the year I played it at the concert. Anyway that was that. Then I went to this next teacher who gave me the upright bass. And he let me take it home over the summer. And my uncle would come by every day. He didn’t have a piano, my mother © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
